newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: S&P upbeat on Argentina, hints at rating upgrade.
newsitem.headline: S&P upbeat on Argentina, hints at rating upgrade.

text.p: Standard & Poor's opened the possibility of an upgrade in Argentina's sovereign debt rating Wednesday through a review of the country's grade and by starting up its first full service site in Latin America in Buenos Aires.

Although Leo O'Neill, president and chief ratings officer of S&P, said there were three possible outcomes of the review, the balance of his comments showed the world's largest rating agency was clearly positive on Argentina's economic prospects.

The three options are an upgrade to the stable outlook on Argentina's BB- long-term foreign currency rating, a straight upgrade or no change. BB- minus is a non-investment grade rating which is below Uruguay, Mexico, Chile and Colombia's.

Asked about the review, the outcome of which is expected in two to three weeks, he told reporters: "I guess in some respects we are putting our money where our mouth is," referring to S&P's purchase of local rating agency Risk Annalysis and the optimism in the country's economy that this purchase reflects.
Argentina will be the rating firm's first full service site in Latin America through the acquisition of Risk Annalysis for an undisclosed sum.

"Buenos Aires represents the most important opportunity for us" in Latin America, said O'Neill, who was visiting Buenos Aires with Harold McGraw III, the president and chief operating officer of McGraw Hill Cos Inc., of which S&P is a division.
S&P has affiliations with a local rating agency in Chile and on Tuesday announced a deal with Brazil's highly respected Getulio Vargas economic institute.
"Rating activities in Argentina have accelerated in the past few years, driven by improving economic and business conditions and by global investor demand for emerging market debt," O'Neill said.
Risk Annalysis was established in 1992 and rates more than 100 government and corporate issuers. It had an affiliation deal with S&P since 1995.
McGraw III said the presence of S&P in Argentina will help "facilitate the capital formation process. Investors are looking for global benchmarks especially in emerging markets."

O'Neill said he was encouraged by Argentina's economy, adding that its history will play a major part in the review. "We are of the opinion that there has been a fundamental change in Argentina and perhaps its history is less indicative of the future than it has been in the past," he said.
Argentina's economy suffered severely in the 1980s as a consequence of hyperinflation which reached nearly 5,000 percent in 1989.

Pointing to the so-called Convertibility plan which has pegged the value of the peso to the dollar since 1991, he said a "steadiness" in policy has emerged. Inflation is low, there is healthy growth and trade has been liberalized, he said.
Growth is seen by the government as rising around five percent this year after an expansion of 4.4 percent in 1996. Inflation was just 0.05 percent last year.
"Is this the way things will be in Argentina for the next indefinite period in time? That is what we are going to have to get comfortable with" through the review, he added.
"I know our sovereign analysis team will weigh the positive economic trends against some continuing fiscal challenges and a relatively high external debt burden in considering the rating," he said.
He also cited continuing labor market rigidities through a failure so far by the government to introduce important labor reforms as a negative factor.
Asked about the importance of corruption in Argentina, O'Neill said: "Not to downplay them, but corruption scandals in themselves do not impact a country's ability to repay debt."

S&P last changed its view on Argentina in March 1995 when in the wake of the Tequila effect -- the term given to the regional ramifications of the December 1994 Mexican peso devaluation -- it changed the outlook on the foreign currency debt rating to stable from positive.
The firm has assigned 25 ratings to Argentine issuers, corporate and government, up from just four three years ago. S&P rates more than $10 trillion worth of the debt of more than 65 countries.
((--Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 318-0668))
